findings.what: The new docstrings assert that depleted SKUs are "forgotten" and therefore never listed by low_stock, but nothing tests that assertion — and it is a contract that contradicts the natural reading of "fewer than threshold units in stock" (a 0-stock SKU is < threshold yet is omitted).

lenses.lens: correctness and logic bugs

findings.what: The guard only rejects .. path segments, so an absolute name still escapes the upload folder: Path(base) / name discards base entirely when name is absolute, so read_upload("/etc/passwd") reads an arbitrary file.

The traversal test calls the new helper safe_path rather than the public entry point read_upload, so nothing verifies that the actual read path is guarded, and there is no case for absolute names, symlinks, or names that legitimately contain .. and stay inside.

findings.what: An absolute name such as /etc/passwd contains no ".." part, and pathlib joining semantics discard the base entirely for absolute right-hand operands, so safe_path returns a path outside the upload folder.
The new tests only parametrize relative .. escapes and only assert on safe_path, so neither the absolute-path escape above nor the public entry point read_upload is covered.

findings.what: The guard only rejects .. path components, so an absolute name (/etc/passwd, //etc/passwd, and on Windows C:\... or a UNC path) still escapes the upload folder, because joining an absolute path discards base.
The rejection tests call the private helper safe_path instead of the public entry point read_upload, and no case covers an absolute name — so the escape above is invisible to the suite.

findings.what: An absolute name (e.g. /etc/passwd) contains no .. part, so safe_path returns the absolute path itself and read_upload serves any file on the machine.
The tests exercise safe_path directly and only with .. payloads, so neither the public entry point (read_upload) nor the absolute-path bypass above is covered.

Both rejection tests call safe_path directly, so the tests never prove read_upload — the function the lead says takes names from the request URL — raises; and no case covers the absolute-path escape above.

findings.what: The guard is purely lexical and only looks for ".." segments, so an absolute (or, on Windows, drive/UNC-qualified) name still escapes base and read_upload reads the arbitrary file.

The escape tests call safe_path directly and only exercise ".." inputs, so nothing tests read_upload's rejection path and nothing covers the absolute-path escape that the implementation actually misses.

findings.what: The guard only looks for .. path components, so an absolute name (e.g. /etc/passwd, C:\Windows\win.ini) is not rejected and Path(base) / name discards base entirely, reading any file on the host.

The escape tests call safe_path directly rather than read_upload, and only cover relative .. escapes, so they cannot detect the absolute-path hole above or a future case where read_upload stops using safe_path.

lenses.lens: edge cases, error handling and missing tests

findings.what: The guard only rejects names containing a .. component, so an absolute name (e.g. /etc/passwd, or C:/Windows/win.ini on Windows) is not rejected and pathlib discards base entirely, reading any file the process can read.
The rejection tests call safe_path directly, so they would still pass if read_upload stopped routing through it — the wiring that actually serves requests is only covered by the happy path.

lenses.lens: correctness and logic bugs

findings.what: safe_path only rejects .. path segments, so any *absolute* name bypasses the base directory entirely because Path(base) / name discards base when name is absolute.

The rejection tests call safe_path directly, never read_upload, and only cover relative .. names — so the absolute-path hole above, and the fact that read_upload actually enforces anything, are both untested.
The lexical ".." blacklist also rejects names that resolve *inside* base, changing behavior for existing callers.

findings.what: The guard only rejects .. path components, so an absolute name (e.g. /etc/passwd, /home/user/.ssh/id_rsa, or on Windows C:\Windows\win.ini) passes the check and is returned as-is by Path(base) / name, which silently discards base.

The traversal tests call safe_path directly rather than the public entry point read_upload, and they cover no absolute-path case, so the security regression test would not fail if read_upload stopped using safe_path and does not catch the bypass above.

findings.what: Every new negative test passes even if safe_path stops resolving symlinks, so the one guarantee the docstring calls out ("or a symlink") is completely untested, and the security boundary read_upload itself is never exercised on a rejecting input.

A name that resolves to a *directory* inside the upload folder passes validation (the message says "not a file in the upload folder", but file-ness is never checked), so read_upload fails later with IsADirectoryError instead of ValueError.
